analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic drug makers to keep cheaper versions off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned pay-for-delay settlements that keep cheaper generic drugs off the market, never got a vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug company challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the brand company sometimes settles the lawsuit by paying the generic maker to stay out of the market for a period of time — an arrangement known as pay-for-delay. That keeps the cheaper generic off the shelves and consumers paying brand-name prices longer. This bill would make those payments illegal under federal trade law, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, with narrow exceptions for settlements that simply let the generic come to market early. It would also tighten the reporting rules so drug companies have to file the complete terms of any settlement, including side deals, under penalty of perjury.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy prescription drugs, including the millions of older Americans on Medicare, would benefit because generics — which typically cost far less than brand-name drugs — would reach the market sooner and more reliably.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug consumers and Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful, unfair method of competition for a brand-name drug company to give a generic filer anything of value in exchange for agreeing not to market the generic drug, with the FTC enforcing the ban the same way it enforces the Federal Trade Commission Act [S3].

Carves out narrow exceptions so settlements are still allowed if the generic gets no more than the right to sell the drug before the patent expires, or a waiver of damages for prior sales — meaning legitimate early-entry deals are preserved [S3].
Lets the FTC exempt agreements it finds pro-competitive and beneficial to consumers, so the ban can be tailored to real competition cases [S3].
Strips a first generic applicant of its 180-day marketing exclusivity if it enters a prohibited agreement, so a company that takes a delay payment loses its government-granted head start [S3].

Requires drug companies to describe any other agreements between the settling parties and to certify, under penalty of perjury, that the filings are the complete and exclusive deal — closing the door on side payments hidden in ancillary contracts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies would lose one of the tools they use to extend the period in which they sell a drug without generic competition, and generic makers could no longer collect settlement payments in exchange for staying out of the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug companies and settling generic makers

drawbacks.text: Not every patent settlement involving payments is anticompetitive; the bill addresses this with an FTC exemption for agreements that further competition and benefit consumers, but critics of pay-for-delay bans have argued that litigation is costly and sometimes a payment is the most efficient way to resolve a genuine patent dispute, and that banning payments could push disputes into lengthy court fights [S3].

Determining whether a settlement includes 'anything of value' in indirect or contingent form can be difficult, which is why the bill also requires certification of complete and exclusive agreements — but companies may still structure deals in ways that are hard to police [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — faster entry of cheaper generic drugs — goes broadly to consumers, and the FTC's enforcement discretion plus the narrow early-entry exception are designed to allow legitimate settlements. The cost falls on the two industries that currently profit from delay arrangements, and the practical trade-off is that some patent disputes that once settled quickly might instead be litigated at length. On balance the design is targeted rather than sweeping: it does not ban settlements, only settlements where the generic is paid not to compete.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and split among three subcommittees, none of which acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on December 11, 2013, joined by Reps. Chris Van Hollen and Henry Waxman [S1][S3].

The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, and within weeks was assigned to the Health, Regulatory Reform Commercial and Antitrust Law, and Courts Intellectual Property and the Internet subcommittees [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and it was left pending at the end of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies keep the ability to settle patent challenges by paying generic makers to delay cheaper competition, and consumers keep paying brand-name prices for longer in those cases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers, which keep the pay-for-delay tool

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no opposition is recorded in the action history, but all six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, so the bill never drew Republican support on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to resolve generic-drug patent challenges by paying the generic maker to stay off the market, which shortens the stretch in which they sell a drug without price competition. Consumers pay the cost of those delay arrangements through higher drug prices.

Generic companies could no longer collect settlement payments for staying out of the market, and a company that took such a deal would forfeit its 180-day exclusivity head start — but generics in general benefit because the bill accelerates market entry for cheaper versions, which is the generic industry's core business.
